title: SDK RPC fidelity layers and prefetch orchestra PRD
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures a pragmatic PRD-level proposal for introducing an SDK-level RPC abstraction that exposes discrete fidelity lanes, first-class prefetch orchestration, and a compact tool-handshake contract for Hosted API streaming calls. The goal is to make it simple for product teams (and third-party integrators) to tune latency vs. cost vs. determinism on a per-invocation basis while preserving observability and a clear migration path from current streaming surfaces.

Context / problem we see in the field:
- Customers want predictable tail latency for interactive flows while still benefiting from batching and KV prefix caching.
- Current streaming SDK surfaces blur the line between partial/early results and committed structured outputs; clients often implement brittle heuristics.
- Tool-calling is fragile across flaky networks: losing the handshake or retries leads to duplicate side effects or silent drops.
- Prefetch logic (speculative warm-up of model/context) exists in multiple ad-hoc places (clients, runtimes, proxies) and is hard to coordinate.

This PRD proposes an SDK RPC that explicitly names: fidelity lanes (fast/light, balanced, faithful), a prefetch orchestration API, and a compact tool-handshake envelope.

Principles:
- Developer ergonomics first: simple defaults, clear opt-in for advanced knobs.
- Observable contracts: each invocation records fidelity lane, prefetch decisions, and tool-handshake events in traces and cost logs.
- Graceful degradation: if prefetch fails or lane unavailable, runtime should fall back to a compatible lane and include reasoning in telemetry.
- Idempotency-first tool calls: SDK should make signature-level guarantees and helpers rather than leaving every safety pattern to app devs.

Goals (measurable):
- Latency: reduce 95th percentile latency for fast/light lane by 30% for short-turn chat prompts (<= 64 tokens).
- Cost: reduce token cost for high-throughput micro-interactions by 20% via coordinated prefix prefetch and light-lane decoding.
- Reliability: eliminate >90% of duplicated tool side-effects caused by network retries in handshake edge-cases.
- Adoption: pilot with 3 internal teams (console, search, customer-success) within Q1 after spec freeze.

Non-goals:
- Full replacement of existing streaming protocol; we aim to be additive and compatible.
- End-to-end runtime changes beyond feature flags and minimal routing heuristics. Runtime-heavy kernel optimization remains separate.

Design overview:
1) Fidelity lanes (client-visible enum)
   - FAST (default): aggressive decoding heuristics, smaller KV caches, favors lower latency; may drop non-essential tokens when system load high.
   - BALANCED: standard production behavior; moderate batching and full prefix caching.
   - FAITHFUL: highest quality, slower; disables lossy heuristics, prefills long context.
   - Transition: SDK exposes a per-call "fidelity" field and a fallthrough policy (fallback_lanes: list).

2) Prefetch orchestra API (SDK primitives)
   - prefetch.profile(name, prompt_fragment, hints) -> prefetch_id
   - prefetch.commit(prefetch_id) to attach prefetch to an invocation, or prefetch.auto_commit TTL semantics.
   - Prefetch requests are best-effort; runtime returns a reason code for misses (prefetch_hit | cold | evicted | denied).
   - Observability: every prefetch has trace_id, start/end, size estimate, and final hit/miss.

3) Compact tool-handshake envelope (structured but minimal)
   - Tool invocation begins with a handshake frame: { tool_id, invocation_id(client-generated), idempotency_key, expected_side_effects: enum }.
   - Runtime responds with handshake_ack: { invocation_id, ephemeral_token, allowed_until } or handshake_nack(reason).
   - Client then streams tool request + input; runtime ensures single delivery semantics when idempotency_key provided (server deduplication window configurable).
   - Retries: after network failure, client may re-issue handshake with same idempotency_key; SDK will surface duplicate-detection callbacks.

4) Structured output and schema layering
   - Return envelope supports streaming partial_payload frames and final_commit frame. Partial frames must include schema_version and a monotonic sequence.
   - SDK provides typed parsers for JSON/YAML/compact-protobuf stubs and a validation helper that can run locally to detect malformed partial frames before presenting to apps.
   - Schema versioning: server advertises supported schema versions in capability header; clients may request a target_schema_version on invocation.

5) SDK ergonomics and default flows
   - High-level APIs: generate(), chat_stream(), call_tool_stream(). Each takes an options bag: { fidelity, prefetch_id?, schema_version?, fallback_lanes? }.
   - Low-level primitives: open_session(), begin_prefetch(), handshake_tool(), send_chunk(), commit(). These are for advanced use-cases.
   - Language SDKs: JS/TS, Python, Go initial parity. JS default to FAST lane for web clients.

Telemetry & observability:
- For each invocation: fidelity_lane, prefetch_id (if used), prefetch_result, handshake_latency, handshake_result, partial_frame_counts, final_commit_latency, cost_estimate (server-provided).
- Integrations: console will show per-route fidelity distributions, prefetch hit rates, and tool-handshake error waterfall.

Migration strategy:
- Phase 0 (behind feature flag): add fidelity field to invocation metadata; no behavioral changes.
- Phase 1: enable prefetch orchestration opt-in (SDK exposes API). Manual pilots.
- Phase 2: default FAST lane for low-cost web tier, measure regressions, rollback if quality drops.

Security & safety considerations:
- Tool handshakes include an expected_side_effects field to help server-side auditing; DO NOT assume this prevents malicious tools — it's advisory and logged.
- Idempotency keys are cryptographically random to reduce collision risk. Server dedup window limited (configurable) and logged.

Examples (JS-like pseudocode):
// simple fast chat
const resp = await client.chat_stream({ fidelity: 'FAST' }, async (chunk) => { render(chunk.text); });

// prefetch usage
const p = await client.prefetch.profile('search-quick', promptSnippet, { anticipate_tokens: 40 });
await client.prefetch.commit(p.id);
const r = await client.generate({ prefetch_id: p.id, fidelity: 'BALANCED' });

// tool call handshake
const inv = client.handshake_tool({ tool_id: 'db-write', idempotency_key: genKey() });
if (inv.ack) { client.send_tool_payload(inv.ephemeral_token, payload); } else { // handle nack }

Open questions / risks (prioritized):
- How expensive are maintaining multiple fidelity queues in serving runtime? (Ask infra/runtime: @Marcus Hsu)
- Prefetch abuse: customers might prefetch large contexts to inflate cache pressure; need quota model.
- UX: what should the SDK do on schema mismatch while streaming? Error early or best-effort present partials?
- How to present prefetch rationale to end-users in console without confusing non-technical audiences?

Next steps / action items:
- [ ] Engineering spike (runtime) to estimate memory and scheduling overhead for fidelity lanes. Owner: Marcus. ETA: 2 weeks.
- [ ] SDK prototype (JS): implement prefetch primitives and handshake mock. Owner: Riley. ETA: 3 weeks.
- [ ] Security review of handshake envelope and idempotency semantics. Owner: Diego. ETA: 1 week.
- [ ] Pilot run with Console team: instrument 2 low-traffic flows. Owner: Product eng lead. ETA: Q1 next sprint.

Appendix (notes / rough experiment ideas):
- Experiment A: FAST lane + tiny-kv (prefetch of last 128 tokens) vs. BALANCED lane without prefetch, measure 95p latency and hallucination rates on question-answer microbenchmarks.
- Experiment B: handshake idempotency window length sweep (30s/120s/600s) and measure duplicate side-effect rate under simulated flakey networks.
